claim: The county commission meets as a board of equalization and review no later than February 1 of the tax year and may adjourn sine die any time after February 15, and must adjourn by the last day of February.
The board fixes property at 60 percent of true and actual value if assessed above or below that, and no assessment may exceed 60 percent of true and actual value.
An assessment may not be increased without at least five days' written notice to the taxpayer.
A person who fails to apply for relief at the board meeting waives the right to seek correction for the current year except on appeal to the Office of Tax Appeals or as otherwise provided.

A taxpayer who elects a hearing before the Board of Equalization and Review may appeal the board's order to the Office of Tax Appeals; the taxpayer's standard of proof is a preponderance of the evidence.
An Office of Tax Appeals petition from a valuation or a Board of Equalization and Review order must be filed by March 31 of the property tax year or it is dismissed as untimely.
An appeal of a Tax Commissioner ruling on taxability or classification must be filed within 30 days after written notice of the ruling.
The former circuit-court relief section for erroneous assessments, §11-3-25, is marked repealed.
Exemption from ad valorem property tax applies to the first $20,000 of assessed value of an owner-occupied homestead used exclusively for residential purposes.
The owner must be 65 or older or certified permanently and totally disabled, and a West Virginia resident for the two consecutive calendar years before the tax year (with stated exceptions).
The exemption attaches to the homestead occupied on the July 1 assessment date and applies to taxes for the following tax year.
If the homestead is transferred by deed, will or otherwise, the $20,000 exemption is removed on the next July 1 assessment date unless the new owner qualifies.
A claim must be filed with the county assessor on or before December 1 following the July 1 assessment day; missing it waives the exemption for the next tax year.
A claimant aged 65 or older need not refile after the first claim unless moving to a new homestead.
State excise tax on transferring title to real estate is $1.10 for each $500 of value or fraction thereof, payable when a document is delivered, accepted or presented for recording.
Beginning July 1, 2025, the tax collected under subsection (a) is a county excise tax retained by the county where collected.
An additional county excise tax of 55 cents per $500 applies, and a county commission may raise it by majority vote to no more than $1.65 per $500.

Only one state tax and one county tax is paid per document, collected where the document is first recorded; the grantor pays unless the grantee accepts the document without payment, in which case the grantee pays.
On a transfer from a trustee or from a county clerk for real estate sold for taxes, the grantee pays the tax.
An additional $20 fee on transfers of real estate for consideration is collected by the clerk before recording and goes to the Affordable Housing Fund.
A transfer on death deed is exempt from the real estate transfer excise tax.

Foreclosure under a deed of trust proceeds by trustee's sale at public auction after default, once conditions precedent in the deed are met.
The trustee publishes notice of sale as a Class II legal advertisement in the county where the property lies.
A copy of the notice is served on the grantor by certified mail, return receipt requested, to the address in the deed of trust or later given in writing.
Subordinate lienholders who previously notified the primary lienholder by certified mail get notice by certified mail at least 20 days before the sale.
The notice must show time and place of sale, parties, deed date, recording book and office, description of the property, and terms of sale.
An action to set aside a trustee's sale for notice or procedural defects must be filed within one year of the sale, provided the grantor was given the required notice.
Section 38-1-8a (trustee's report with additional information) applies to deeds of trust on property occupied or intended as the grantor's residence.
The clerk's fee for a trustee's report of sale subject to §38-1-8a is $40.

A 'small asset' does not include real estate or an interest in real property.
For the small estate test, real estate value is presumed to be 167 percent of current assessed value on the county land books.
A testate estate whose will directs real estate to be sold (not a mere power to sell) is not a small estate.

A $1 fee applies for each additional page on documents over five pages.
The clerk admits a deed to record when acknowledged by the signer or proved by two witnesses before the clerk.

By September 10 each year the sheriff prepares a second list of delinquent real estate still delinquent on September 1, with notice of sale.
The notice states the lands will be certified to the Auditor on October 31 and tax liens sold at public auction to the highest bidder for not less than taxes, interest and charges.
Before certification, delinquent property is redeemed by paying the sheriff taxes, interest and charges; after certification and before sale, by paying the Auditor.
A $25 list charge and $10 per addressee mailing charge are added to amounts due.
The sheriff must mail notice of delinquency and sale date by certified mail at least 30 days before the Auditor's sale to owners and lienholders.
The Auditor certifies the list of lands subject to sale on or after March 1 and on or before August 1 each year, adding a $25 charge per tract.
West Virginia sells tax liens at public auction; unsold tracts may be sold by the Auditor without further advertising or auction.
After a tax lien sale, the owner or a lienholder may redeem at any time before a tax deed is issued.
Redemption requires taxes, interest and charges due at sale plus interest at one percent per month from sale, taxes the purchaser paid, statutory costs, and the Auditor's fee.
Title examination and notice-list expenses charged to the redeeming owner are capped at $500 excluding interest.
An owner may petition the Auditor to redeem a primary residence in installments for financial hardship; the notice to redeem describes up to three incremental payments.
The Auditor's notice to redeem states the date on or after which a deed will be made unless the property is redeemed.
The grantee pays the transfer tax on a deed from a county clerk for real estate sold for taxes.

An owner or agent may petition the magistrate court or circuit court in the county for summary relief by verified petition for rent arrears, breach of covenant, or damage.
The court sets a hearing not less than five nor more than 10 judicial days after the petition is filed.
The notice of hearing is served per Rule 4 or certified mail; the tenant may file a written defense within five days of receipt.
If the tenant files no response, the court shall grant immediate possession to the landlord.
The order sets the time to vacate, after which the sheriff removes the tenant.
A landlord may dispose of stored or left personal property after 30 days under conditions stated in §55-3A-3(h).
A tenant may raise any defense available in ejectment or unlawful detainer.
A year-to-year tenancy may be ended by written notice at least three months before the end of the year; a shorter periodic tenancy by notice of one full period before its end.
Notice is not required where a special agreement fixes another period or none, or for a tenant whose term ends at a certain time.
An owner or agent has a summary remedy to recover possession from a tenant wrongfully occupying.

West Virginia requires income tax withholding on sales of West Virginia real property by nonresident sellers.
Withholding is either 2.5% of the total payment to the nonresident or 4.58% of estimated capital gain.
The nonresident return NRSR must be submitted with payment within 30 days of withholding.
Exceptions include resident transferors, foreclosure or deed in lieu, governmental agency transferors, and a transferor's principal residence.

An individual may transfer property to one or more beneficiaries effective at death by a transfer on death deed.
The deed must meet the formalities of a recordable inter vivos deed, state the transfer occurs at death, and be recorded before death with the county clerk where the property lies.
It is exempt from the real estate transfer excise tax because the deed is revocable and passes no interest at recording.
During the transferor's life the deed does not affect the transferor's right to transfer or encumber the property, nor create any interest in the beneficiary.
The article applies to TOD deeds made on or after its effective date by transferors dying on or after that date.
